content: Chronic mountain sickness (CMS), also referred to as Monge's disease, was first described in 1925 by Carlos Monge. High Altitude Flatus Expulsion, another phenomenon related to high altitude, was initially documented by Joseph Hamel around 1820 and later rediscovered in 1981 by Paul Auerbach and York Miller. Altitude sickness is categorized into two main groups: acute and chronic. This classification is based on clinical symptoms and the pathological changes in the affected organs. Hypoxia, or low oxygen levels, stimulates the body to increase oxygen delivery to tissues by enhancing ventilation, cardiac output, and hemoglobin concentrations. These physiological adaptations improve ventilation-perfusion matching and gas exchange but can also lead to high-altitude pulmonary hypertension. Risk factors for developing altitude sickness include pre-existing lung disease, conditions or substances that impair acclimatization, a prior history of altitude sickness, and inadequate acclimatization. Globally, the incidence of altitude sickness is approximately 53,000 cases per 100,000 individuals. The prevalence and mortality rates vary depending on altitude, with most cases reported in regions such as Kilimanjaro and the Everest region of Nepal. While individuals of all ages can develop altitude sickness, the incidence increases with age, with a median age of diagnosis between 26 and 45 years. There is no racial predisposition to the condition. Routine screening for altitude sickness is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. Common screening methods, such as the cold pressor test, heart rate variability, and pulmonary function tests, are not routinely utilized. The natural history of altitude sickness can lead to complications such as high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) and cerebral edema. Despite these potential complications, the prognosis is generally favorable, with a five-year mortality rate of approximately 12%. Common symptoms include headache, dizziness, fatigue, and cyanosis. Physical examination findings may include nausea, vomiting, and lightheadedness. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings may include a shortened R-R interval, changes in the Q-T interval, ST-T flattening, and an increase in P wave amplitude. Imaging studies can aid in the diagnosis of altitude sickness and its complications. Chest X-rays may reveal patchy alveolar infiltrates, predominantly in the right central hemithorax, and asymmetric airspace consolidation. CT scans can also demonstrate similar findings, particularly in cases of pulmonary edema. MRI may show increased T2 signal in the white matter of the splenium of the corpus callosum in cases of high-altitude cerebral edema. No additional imaging or diagnostic studies are specifically associated with altitude sickness. Pharmacologic treatments for altitude sickness include acetazolamide and dexamethasone. For nausea and vomiting associated with the condition, medications such as promethazine and ondansetron are effective. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing altitude sickness. Primary prevention strategies include avoiding alcohol, consuming a high-carbohydrate diet, maintaining adequate hydration, limiting vigorous physical activity during the initial days at high altitude, and using oxygen enrichment. To further understand susceptibility to high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), the International HAPE Database was established in 2004. Individuals with a history of HAPE can register with this confidential database to assist researchers in studying the condition.
